response.task_summary: Predict whether an NHANES participant has high cholesterol using stable cardiometabolic risk factors while avoiding reliance on survey-cycle or demographic/domain shortcuts.

ranking.rationale: Age is one of the most stable and strongest predictors of cholesterol risk across domains.
History of hypertension is a robust cardiometabolic correlate of high cholesterol.
Diagnosed diabetes strongly tracks metabolic syndrome and dyslipidemia.
Absence of hypertension remains informative because it lowers expected cholesterol risk.
No diabetes is still predictive as a protective metabolic indicator.
Sex has a biologically meaningful and fairly stable relationship with cholesterol patterns.
Prediabetes captures early metabolic dysfunction relevant to cholesterol.
No prediabetes still helps distinguish lower metabolic risk.
Kidney disease is clinically linked to abnormal lipid metabolism and vascular risk.
No kidney disease is informative as a lower-risk health profile.
Arthritis can proxy older age and chronic inflammation, both related to cholesterol risk.
No arthritis modestly indicates a healthier and often younger profile.
Recent dialysis indicates severe kidney disease, a meaningful but rarer correlate.
No dialysis modestly helps separate lower renal-risk participants.
Psoriasis is associated with systemic inflammation and somewhat elevated cardiometabolic risk.
No psoriasis is weakly informative in the opposite direction.
Borderline diabetes may capture intermediate metabolic risk relevant to cholesterol.
Very low education can reflect stable socioeconomic influences on diet and healthcare access.
College graduation is a broad socioeconomic marker that may generalize somewhat for health behaviors.
Some college carries moderate socioeconomic signal related to preventive health and diet.
High school completion provides modest socioeconomic information relevant to cholesterol risk.
Less than high school is a modest but plausible predictor through social determinants.
Marital status may weakly proxy household stability and health behaviors, though less robustly.
Alternative marital categories can carry small lifestyle and support-network signals.
Marital status remains only weakly predictive but may capture behavior differences.
Another marital category with limited but possible association to health management.
Separated status may weakly reflect stress or lifestyle differences, but is brittle.
Never married status has limited direct causal relevance beyond age and lifestyle proxies.
Country of birth may correlate with diet and access patterns, but risks demographic shortcutting.
US-born status is similarly weak and potentially domain-specific rather than causal.
Refused education response is mostly a missingness artifact with little semantic value.
Don't know education response is largely noise and may encode survey behavior.
Don't know/refused hypertension response is mostly response-style information, not stable biology.
Don't know/refused diabetes response is weak and likely reflects survey artifact.
Don't know/refused prediabetes response has little stable predictive meaning.
Don't know/refused kidney disease response is mostly nonresponse behavior.
Don't know/refused psoriasis response is likely noise rather than transportable signal.
Don't know/refused arthritis response is mainly a survey-response artifact.
Refused marital status is mostly nonresponse and may encode domain-specific survey patterns.
Don't know marital status has little semantic relevance to cholesterol.
Refused country-of-birth response is mostly a demographic nonresponse artifact.
Don't know country-of-birth response is weak and potentially domain-linked.
Missing hypertension data may reflect collection patterns more than participant risk.
Missing diabetes data is mostly a survey-process artifact with limited transportability.
Missing prediabetes data likely reflects questionnaire routing or nonresponse.
Missing kidney disease data is unlikely to be a stable causal predictor.
Missing dialysis data is mostly procedural and rare.
Missing psoriasis data is weakly informative and likely survey-specific.
Missing arthritis data is mostly nonsemantic missingness.
Missing education may encode survey administration differences more than health risk.
Missing marital status is largely a nonresponse artifact.
Missing country of birth is mostly demographic nonresponse and not a stable predictor.
Survey year is a likely domain identifier and should be strongly penalized for OOD generalization.
